title: Spielberg to Scorsese - “you are the master of our medium, and this is your masterpiece.” KOTFM is great, but far from Scorsese’s best film.

commenti.body: [removed]

It’s definitely in his top ten. It’s too hard to it’s its place beyond that given we can’t huge cultural
Impact, staying power, etc. 

But I don’t think it’s out of pocket to say it’s his best either. This is a great film. And it shows an evolution on Marty’s part that’s pretty awe inspiring. At his age he’s still iterating, still finding new boundaries to push. 

It explores the same themes he’s spent his career exploring while feeling totally new and not at all like he retreading old ground.

i think Spielberg is probably way past his prime and doesn’t really care about quality anymore. 

I have friends in Hollywood and there’s quite a few rumours about how Spielberg is kind of a giant asshole now and only cares about money and awards. I obviously have no idea if this is true or not, but it seems plausible. 

I think if Spielberg can convince himself KOTFM is Scorsese’s best work, which i agree was good but by no means his best, then maybe Spielberg can convince himself that Fabelmans or whatever his next project will be his best work.

>I obviously have no idea if this is true or not

The only relevant thing you said

They’ve both reached a status of being collectively jerked-off by Hollywood to the point that they’ll be praised no matter what they do.

Their peak years are long gone. They’re still great filmmakers (obviously), but my focus is on fresh perspectives. Ari Aster, Robbert Eggers, Brandon Cronenberg, Park Chan-Wook, etc.

He’s just hyping up his colleague, it’s not that complicated. What, you expect him to say “Now I really liked your newest movie, but it’s not even in your top 5” right to Scorsese’s face? Why would he do that?
That's a Ridley Scott move haha

It’s a top five film for Scorsese for me. It’s a culmination of all his knowledge and it shows. He’s at the top of his craft and poured all his passion into telling this complex event. It might not be an easy rewatch like his other films cause of the subject matter, but it’s an important one that has something to say.

Wow, you really went deep in there,  inside of an imaginary version of Steven Spielberg, pulled out a lot of imaginary thoughts and turned it into assumptions to judge the entirety of the man. 

So much creativity wasted so badly.

KOTFM is not going to be remembered as a great film just like The Irishman will not be remembered either. DiCaprio's acting is the most memorable part of the movie. He's probably the most talented leading male actor working today. Not saying he's the best actor in the world.

I think Spielberg is boosting KOTFM because it's Scorsese's current film. It's not promotion but we don't know how long either of those filmmakers will be around for and how many more movies they'll make. Would it be relevant/would there be as much coverage if Spielberg discussed Raging Bull/Goodfellas/take your pick from MS's filmography? No.

Scorsese's film-making is no longer lean and taught, his movies are now like an out of shape body which sags and is overweight. Considering he has the same career long editor I'm surprised Thelma doesn't enforce a shorter runtime.

Having read the book of KOTFM I knew it was gonna be near impossible to make a decent adaptation of it and they really do only adapt one third of the book. 

The film is miscast as well. De Niro is far, far too old for his role (by at least 30 years). DiCaprio is too old for his character and should have been cast in DeNiro's role.

I had read the adaptation really struggled until DiCaprio realised he had to play the husband and not the investigator that Jesse Plemons plays. It would have been a very different movie. 

While the movie is executed well (pun-intended) my issue is that it's not a good screenplay mainly because its a near impossible to adapt into a feature. Scorsese should have made a longform series out of it instead.

I don't think KOTFM is Scorsese's greatest, but I know some people who consider it to be among his top 3 or so films. More importantly, Marty himself considers the movie to be very important to him and always mentions how he has started to view the art form differently in his old age. I absolutely love Marty's last three films which I kind of consider to be influenced by his changed outlook, and I don't believe that calling anyone one of these movies to be his masterpiece is ridiculous. In fact, there are not much more than a handful of his movies of which I would think calling them his masterpiece would be ridiculous.

Man, even Steven Spielberg will get downvoted for his opinion of his friend's film on /truefilm! 

I loved KotFM. If someone else did, I get it. If someone else didn't love it, or don't consider it among their favorite Scorsese pictures, that's perfectly OK. I guess I get their perspective too. After all, this is one of the great filmmakers we are talking about. We'll all have our preferences. Just focus on what your preference is.
What? Both will be remembered as great films, they just won't be considered Top 5. Maybe Flower Moon, but people cannot get over Irishman's de aging.
Park Chan-wook is 60 years old and has been directing for 31 years.

I strongly disagree about KOTFM. Irishman whatever. But I think KOTFM is so odd and strange and weirdly subtle that over time it will be seen very well. But in any event you don't know and neihter do I, it's so hard to predict.

One thing I disagree with is the idea the film is "like an out of shape body which sags and is overweight". Something fascinating about the movie is how non-showy it is. I don't agree his films have ever been that lean or taught but they were certainly showy. With Flowers he has evolved into a style that is so calm. Still full of stunning images but never shower or show-off. The camera is so intentional. It's very interesting!

I'd say to call this judgement "bizarre" is "a bit of an overreach".

You concede that it is a great movie, so why would you be so puzzled that it's at the top of his list? To quibble about the exact ranking sequence of a filmmaker's oeuvre is a vain and silly exercise, and there's no reason to believe that your ranking would be any more "accurate" than Spielberg's or mine or Tommy Wiseau's.

Flower Moon **clearly** is the work of a master of his craft. That is true for at least two dozen of Scorsese's movies. How much it does or doesn't appeal to your personal sensibilities will decide where exactly you'll rank it, and knowing Spielberg's sensibilities it isn't surprising at all that it comes in first.

Honestly this thread is so indicative of why this sub drives me batty. 

Half the time, you get some of the best film analysis you can find on the internet and the other half you get these willfully dense meta-threads that are reacting to the reaction to a film rather than the film itself.

A peer is complimenting a peer at a public event. Steven Spielberg is not making some grand statement and even if he was, that’s his opinion. Are you *seriously* calling his judgment into question because he likes a movie more than you did?

This is the obvious answer plus this is still marketing. The film just came out on PVOD and Spielberg knows exactly what he is doing. Someone reads an article about how the great Steven Spielberg says this film is a masterpiece and they might go "damn I need to watch that"

I think what he means by this is that in watching it I could tell it was a film maker fully aware of the choices he is making and how they affect the story visually. Like Tarantino’s Once Upon a Time a Time it isn’t the film makers “best” film because that is subjective but the idea of what makes it “best” for one filmmaker to another is the power with which the story is told visually and how strongly those devices are used.  It’s like Kafka’s writings. They are powerful in a way I always felt he was siphoning from a source and not creating on his own. Like he’s his hand on a lighting bolt and doing what he can with what he can from that moment. But he never seemed to bottle the lighting. And I would say if you could bottle lighting like it seems Scorsese did with this film then that lightning loses a lot of what made it so awe inspiring.

lol. as opposed to the rest of the comments on here where they’re just asking Spielberg what he thinks?

I’m sure your all working very hard on your next screenplay. 😂

maybe one day someone will explain what a conjecture or opinion is.  You do realize that you also have no idea if this is true, right? No one here has any idea why Spielberg said what he said. Nor can we. I was just telling an anecdote based on people i know who’ve met him. Lol. You guys are ridiculous.

KOTFM might be considered a great film in the future when re-appraisals happen in a decade or 20/25 years. Perhaps my view will change as it will be that long since I read the book and I can perhaps see it only as the film not an adaptation. 

The movie is certainly well-crafted. 

I doubt I'm ever gonna change my mind on De Niro being so much older for the role than the actor should be. But Martin wants to work with Bobby so we get 80 year old De Niro as a lead character again.

The Irishman is never gonna be considered a great film. It will likely rank mid-way out of Scorsese's filmography. Better than his awful remake of Cape Fear but not close to his excellent work in the 1970s and 1980s.
